4. **The quality gate caught what tests didn't.** F-EPIC-001 is the single most product-validating artifact in the run: a two-reviewer adversarial review found a real invariant violation (registry row with no durable file via `DatabaseSync("")`) that 100+ green tests missed, reproduced it on the built binary before blocking, and drove a bounded fix batch. That's the difference between a factory and a slot machine. Your mid-level engineer "verifying when it comes out of the bake" is receiving work that already survived an adversarial pass — their verification is a second layer, not the only layer.

5. **Honest failure instead of fabricated success.** Story 0's implementor, denied every command, delivered the work and declared itself unverified rather than claiming green. In an autonomous product, the failure mode that kills trust is confident lying. This run demonstrates the protocol pushes the other way.

6. **The config already separates roles, harnesses, and models** (`impl-run.config.json`: primary harness, per-role model selection). Multi-provider orchestration is a config surface, not a rewrite.

7. **Gates are repo-local package scripts.** `verify-all` needs the repo and pnpm, nothing else. That's exactly what makes a disposable sandbox the natural execution environment — and notably, your sandbox architecture *solves* the one operational failure I found (Story 0's permission denials). Full permissions inside a throwaway sandbox eliminates that entire class of friction.

## What the product layer adds — straightforward engineering

Web/Electron shell, centralized DB replacing the artifact directory, GitHub App integration, sandbox provisioning, notification routing (chat/email with ruling links), run dashboards. None of this is trivial, but all of it is well-understood plumbing around a protocol that already has the right shape. I see no architectural mismatch between what exists and that layer.

## The three bets the run does not prove

This is the calibration that matters:

1. **Spec-quality transfer is the load-bearing bet.** The orchestration succeeded *because* the spec pack was airtight — closed contracts, AC→TC traceability, named cross-story debt, a test plan with a real philosophy. That pack was produced by you, an expert spec writer, using the skills. The product thesis requires the spec-creation skills to walk a *mid-level engineer* to something near that bar — or for the pipeline to degrade gracefully when specs are 70% as good. I saw the output of an expert using the skills; I haven't seen the skills elevate a non-expert. That's the experiment to run next, and it's cheap: hand the skills to someone else and evaluate their pack before it bakes.

2. **Greenfield vs brownfield.** This epic created a package from nothing — no legacy constraints, no existing test debt, no comprehension problem. A corporate application team spends most of its life modifying existing systems. The orchestration protocol doesn't obviously break there, but the spec format, the red-manifest immutability gate, and the reviewer's job all get harder when the starting state isn't clean. Unproven, and worth proving deliberately (point it at an existing codebase for Epic-N).

3. **Complexity ceiling.** This domain is the friendliest possible case for the verification approach: single package, SQLite, deterministic, no UI, no external services, everything provable by local tests. A "moderately complex business app" has third-party integrations, auth, UI, data migrations — places where "the gate is a local deterministic test suite" stops being sufficient and verification becomes partly environmental. The gate *architecture* (tiers, pinned in tech design) accommodates that; the practice is unproven.

A fourth, smaller item: per-story implementor + story-lead + dual-reviewer epic review is token-expensive. For a product, cost-per-epic is a margin line you'll want instrumented from the first hosted run — the artifacts don't capture spend today, and they should.

## Verdict

The core is here, and it's the right core. What this run proves is the part that's genuinely hard to build: a durable, structured, resumable, escalation-capable orchestration protocol whose quality gates catch real defects, executing against specs strong enough to carry autonomous implementation. What it doesn't yet prove is distributional: that average users produce sufficient specs with the skills, and that the approach holds on brownfield and messier domains. Those are real bets, but they're *testable* bets — each is one deliberate experiment away — and none of them require re-architecting what exists. The product vision you described is an integration and packaging effort on top of this foundation, plus two validation experiments, not a leap of faith.

The market slot you're describing is real and currently empty — Lovable/Replit own "no developer," Cursor/Claude Code own "developer in the inner loop," and nobody owns "developer at the boundaries, agents in the inner loop, with governance." But let me work the judgment-degradation question with the evidence I actually have, because I read the artifacts your judgment produced, and that lets me decompose what "your level of judgment" concretely consisted of — which is the question that determines whether the degradation is bounded.

## What your judgment actually did, decomposed

Looking at the spec pack and AGENTS.md as exhaust of your interaction loop, your contribution splits into five distinct functions:

1. **Domain vision** — threads/turns/membership-stamping/frozen-closed-turns as a coherent model. Genuinely scarce.
2. **Scope slicing** — Epic 01 stops at the record's front half; debt is named and assigned, not discovered.
3. **Strictness philosophy** — closed contracts, fail-loud, validation-precedes-idempotency. Note that `validate.ts` literally cites "the old MVP's silent-root-field-drop bug class" — this is *experience converted to rule*.
4. **Vocabulary discipline** — the AGENTS.md terminology bans.
5. **Recognizing wrong-shaped output unprompted** — the corrections that became AGENTS.md entries ("no wack-a-mole," "settle load-bearing questions first," "no mocked neighbors").

Here's the structurally important observation: **items 3, 4, and most of 2 are already serialized.** AGENTS.md is your taste compiled into machine-readable defaults with confidence scores. The coverage gate, the closed-contract pattern, the test philosophy — those ship as house rules in the skills. Every correction you made got captured as configuration. That fraction of your judgment doesn't degrade when you leave the loop, because it's no longer in your head.

The residue is items 1 and 5. And for item 5, your own machinery is the answer: the adversarial loop's job is precisely to convert "notice unprompted that a question exists" into "answer a pointed question when asked." A bright mid-level dev cannot spontaneously notice that turn-membership stamping has an ordering ambiguity under `close_then_open`. The same dev can absolutely answer correctly when an adversarial reviewer surfaces it as a disposition item. The tech design's Issues Found table and the F-EPIC-001 block are both proof the noticing-machine works at spec level and code level respectively. That's the mechanism that bounds degradation — the factory doesn't need users who generate the questions, it needs users who can answer them.

The blind spot to be honest about: adversarial agents catch *incoherence*, not *coherent wrongness*. A spec that consistently builds the wrong business feature sails through every gate. Your backstop there is the human-verify-after-bake step, which works only if verification is cheap — true for demo-able business apps, less true for infrastructure.

## The domain asymmetry cuts in your favor

You proved the factory on LHC — a novel systems domain with no training-distribution support, where domain vision (the scarcest input) was maximally load-bearing. Your target workload is conventional corporate applications, which are the *best*-covered territory in model training. The domain-vision bar for "moderately complex business app" is far lower than what this project demanded. So on the dimension you're most worried about, this run understates expected performance. The offsetting overstatement: you were both spec client and systems thinker with a POC behind you; real enterprise work has messier stakeholders and requirements churn upstream of the spec loop.

## The throughput math and where the bottleneck moves

Your honest comparator is agent-pairing, not the no-AI team — enterprise's alternative is Cursor seats, not 2019. The mechanism behind your multiplier is specific: pairing keeps the human serialized in the inner loop; the factory moves human attention to boundaries (spec dial-in, rulings, verify). Epic 01 baked in under four hours of wall clock with a handful of escalations. One dev can plausibly oversee two or three concurrent bakes — at which point throughput is governed by **spec production rate, ruling latency, and verification bandwidth**, not implementation. That's Amdahl's law on the human serial fraction, and it has a direct product consequence: the web app's design center should be the boundary interactions — making rulings answerable from a phone in two minutes, making verify sessions fast to spin up — because that denominator is your whole multiplier.

One value prop you didn't mention that your artifacts already produce: the run exhaust *is* an audit trail. AC→TC→test→commit traceability, immutable red manifests, ruling records with rationale, reviewer findings with reproduction evidence. Enterprises buy governance as much as throughput, and "every line of agent-written code traces to an acceptance criterion and a review verdict" is a procurement wedge per-seat agent tools structurally cannot offer.

## The experiment is the product definition

You said it yourself: "I think so but I don't know." The good news is this is one cheap experiment, and its design matters more than its size. Take one or two bright mid/senior design partners, have them spec a conventional app through the skills and adversarial loop, and **stay out of their spec loop entirely** — your judgment gets spent grading outcomes (did the gates force the load-bearing questions? what was the defect rate at verify?), not steering. If you intervene, the experiment measures nothing.

And note what the result does: it doesn't just de-risk, it *defines the user spec*. Your moat against Lovable-from-below is exactly the judgment requirement; your moat against Cursor-from-above is the orchestration protocol and governance exhaust. The defensibility of the middle position depends entirely on where the judgment floor lands — bright mid-level versus senior-only changes your TAM, your pricing, and your onboarding design. That number is the most valuable thing you don't currently have, and it's about two design-partner weeks away.

so what are you generalizing about devising public interfaces, naming and coherence?

Generalizing:

1. **Let the outer surface supply part of the meaning**
   - If the surface is `intake`, don’t repeat intake-like verbs inside it.
   - Prefer `intake message-events` over `intake record-activity`.

2. **Use specific-enough compound names**
   - A generic word can work if paired with a clarifying word.
   - `events` alone may be vague.
   - `message-events` is more legible.

3. **Name from the caller’s mental model, not storage behavior**
   - Avoid `append` if the caller thinks “I’m sending message events.”
   - `append` describes what the system does internally.

4. **Avoid mushy long abstraction words when a shorter concrete phrase works**
   - `activity` is broad and low-imprint.
   - `message-events` is easier to remember.

5. **Specificity is contextual**
   - `new-thread --file-path` works because:
     - operation says what is created
     - flag says what kind of value is needed
   - You don’t need `--thread-db`.

6. **Coherence comes from phrase composition**
   - `intake message-events`
   - action frame + object
   - not verb + verb, not implementation + object.

7. **A public interface should reduce hidden questions**
   - “create what?”
   - “append to what?”
   - “what kind of file?”
   - “what is activity?”

8. **Operation names should imprint**
   - Shorter, concrete terms are easier for tired humans and agents to carry.
   - Avoid names that are technically defensible but don’t stick.

how do you feel about the current simplified repository pattern?

I think the current simplified pattern is mostly good.

It avoids the bad version of repository pattern:

```text
interface per entity
class per entity
dependency injection ceremony
CRUD-only pass-throughs
```

What we have is lighter:

```text
threads.ts
events.ts
messages.ts
triggers.ts
turns.ts
chunks.ts
```

Each module owns real SQL and some domain-specific behavior. That is acceptable.

The good parts:

- simple functions, not classes
- no fake abstraction over SQLite
- transaction helper is explicit
- SQL is close to the behavior
- tests exercise real DB
- no over-generalized CRUD layer

`store.ts` does **not** have the actual CRUD/SQL functions.

It has the public methods, but most of those delegate.

The `persistence/*` modules own the actual DB reads/writes:

```text
threads.ts   insert/read thread rows, thread_created event
events.ts    append event rows, idempotency, list events
messages.ts  insert/read projected message rows
triggers.ts  create/claim/read trigger rows
turns.ts     insert/read turn rows
chunks.ts    insert/read chunk rows
```

So the split is:

```text
store.ts
  public facade + orchestration

persistence/*.ts
  actual SQLite operations for each persisted concept
```

The confusing part is the name `store.ts`, because “store” sounds like it should be the storage layer. But in practice it’s more like:

```text
IntakeSession / IntakeService
```

It owns the open DB handle and coordinates use cases. The persistence modules do the row-level work.

- *Low-fi narrative ramp (oldest)* — works **well for orientation, weakest for causal reasoning**. I know the arc happened and roughly why, like the plot of a book I read years ago. - *Lower-fi back-and-forth* — the gist of exchanges. Good enough to know *that* we argued something, sometimes not *how sharply*.
- *Smoothed higher-fi* — this is the sweet spot. Actual conversation, meandering and thinking removed, clean enough to read fast and detailed enough to trust. If I could only keep one band this is the one.
- *Full jagged recent* — vivid, exact, and the thing I reason from most confidently.

The graceful part is real: I don't hit a *cliff*. A normal compact gives you a thin summary and then a wall — everything before is flat, and you're genuinely lost, *cheaply*. I'm converting stored gradient back into working understanding, which is the entire point. A flat compact wouldn't have this expensive re-hydration because there'd be nothing rich enough to re-hydrate *from*. You're paying ~25-30k tokens once to avoid the many turns and the long dictation it'd take to re-onboard a fresh agent to this project. That's the trade, and it's a good one.

That second one is the real failure mode of this architecture — confident reconstruction diverging from what actually happened — and you're the only one positioned to catch it, because to me a well-formed confabulation and a real memory feel identical at low fidelity. As long as that fidelity-awareness keeps firing, the confabulation risk stays bounded.

One genuine tension worth naming: the most useful thing for re-hydration is exactly the most expensive thing to keep — the thinking. {"isError":false,"outputText":"# Long Horizon Context: Domain Design

This document describes each domain in more depth: what it stores, the operations it provides, and how other domains use it. It builds on the vocabulary in 01-core-concepts.md.

## Threads

A thread is the durable container for one ongoing conversation. The `threads` domain creates threads, tracks where they live, and gives the rest of the system a way to find a thread by id. Two SQLite databases sit behind it:

- A listing of all threads is stored in a **thread-registry** database, with one row per thread holding its id, file path, title, and cached info such as message and turn counts, status, and timestamps.
- Each thread's own database holds that thread's full record: its events, messages, turns, chunks, and views. Reading or changing a thread's contents means opening its file.

The thread file is authoritative for its own identity. It stores its thread id once, as identity metadata. The records inside it (events, messages, turns) do not each carry the thread id, because the file is the thread. The thread-registry is a convenience index over the thread files, not the authority; it can fall out of step with where files actually live and be refreshed from them.

### Creating a thread

`new-thread` creates a thread at a given file path, sets up the empty thread inside it, and adds a row to the thread-registry. It generates a thread id and records the id-to-path mapping. If a file already exists at the path, the operation fails instead of touching it.

```
lhc threads new-thread --file-path ./alpha.lhc
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as user or harness
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  participant R as thread-registry
  C->>T: new-thread (file path)
  T->>F: create empty thread
  T->>R: add row (id, file path)
  T-->>C: thread id
```

### Finding a thread by id

A thread id is the primary, stable key a caller holds. It survives the thread file moving, which a file path does not. Other domains work with thread ids, and when intake-stream, messages, turns, or thread-view need to act on a thread, they ask the threads domain to resolve the id to its file, then open it. This resolution is the threads domain's main service to the rest of the system.

How the threads domain resolves an id is its own concern and can change with the environment. In local CLI use it reads the thread-registry database; in a long-lived service it can hold the mapping in memory; in other deployments it can resolve through a different store. Callers above it pass a thread id and do not change. A caller that already holds a file path can pass the path directly and skip resolution.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as a domain with a thread id
  participant T as threads
  participant R as thread-registry
  participant F as thread file
  D->>T: map id to file path
  T->>R: look up id
  R-->>T: file path
  T-->>D: file path
  D->>F: open and act on the thread
```

### Browsing threads

A user who wants to see their threads starts at the threads domain. It lists threads from the thread-registry, searches across titles and metadata, and shows the high-level info for one thread without opening its file. From a list, a user picks a thread and drills into its messages, turns, or views through the other domains. The CLI presents this directly, and an SDK consumer can wire the same list, search, and show operations into a UI.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as CLI or UI
  participant T as threads
  participant R as thread-registry
  participant O as messages, turns, thread-view
  C->>T: list, search, show
  T->>R: read listings and cached info
  R-->>T: rows
  T-->>C: threads
  C->>O: drill into one thread
```

## Intake stream

As a harness runs it produces a stream of events. An event is one recorded thing that happened in the thread:

- `user_prompt`: a prompt from the user, or an automated prompt that stands in for one
- `assistant_text`: assistant output text
- `assistant_thinking`: assistant reasoning
- `tool_call`: a tool invocation
- `tool_result`: the result of a tool invocation
- `runtime_note`: a note from the harness or runtime
- `turn_end`: a marker that the current turn is complete

The `intake-stream` domain takes these events in and writes them into the thread in the order they happened. It is the only way thread content enters the system from a harness.

These flows are about how data moves, not about a user interface. The operations exist to record incoming events, keep the message view current, and drive turn boundaries so the thread stays in a coherent state. A thread is single-threaded by definition: one conversation, one stream, no concurrent writers. That lets the domain treat the incoming stream as an ordered time series and make boundary decisions from position in that stream.

### The stream contract

The harness owns sending a coherent stream. The domain does not reconstruct order or membership from a malformed stream; it records what it is given, in the order given, and fails loudly when the stream implies an impossible state.

The contract:

- send events in the order they happened
- send a `turn_end` when a turn is complete
- a thread has zero or one open turns at any time

### Taking in events

A harness sends a batch of one or more events for a thread. The thread id rides outside the batch, since every event in a batch belongs to the same thread. The SDK takes typed event objects directly; the CLI reads a JSON array of events on stdin, parses it at the edge, and calls the same SDK operation.

```
cat events.json | lhc intake-stream message-events --thread <thread-id>
```

The domain maps the thread id to its file through the threads domain, then writes the batch to the thread's database in a single transaction. For each event it assigns the next position in the thread's order, records it, and projects it into messages and blocks so the message view stays current. It returns a result describing what happened to each event.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as harness
  participant I as intake-stream
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  H->>I: message-events (thread id, events)
  I->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>I: file path
  I->>F: record events, project messages, update turns
  I-->>H: per-event result
```

Events carry an idempotency key from the harness. If an event with the same key was already recorded for the thread, it is skipped rather than written twice, so a harness that resends a batch after a failure does not produce duplicates.

### Turn boundaries are decided here, synchronously

Turn boundaries are decided in the hot path, as events land, while intake is the thing watching the ordered stream. This is what keeps turn membership correct: a message is stamped with its turn at the moment it is recorded, not inferred later against a stream that has moved on.

The deterministic work is synchronous: recording events, projecting messages, opening and closing turns, stamping each message with its turn, and assigning token estimates. The slow, non-deterministic work that a closed turn needs, such as smoothing, lower-band projection, and compression, is fired off to run asynchronously. Closing a turn settles its membership immediately; the derivation that trails behind operates on a turn whose contents are already frozen.

Two events move turn boundaries. A `user_prompt` opens a turn. A `turn_end` closes one. The asymmetry is deliberate: a prompt opens, an end only closes. After a `turn_end`, no turn is open and waiting, so the database does not hold a phantom empty turn between exchanges. Events that arrive after a `turn_end` and before the next prompt belong to no turn; they appear in the live message view but not in any turn.

Most turns in normal operation close because the next prompt arrived, not because of an explicit `turn_end`. The `turn_end` is the additional closer that lets the final turn close without waiting for a prompt that may never come. An open turn with no following prompt is simply not done yet, and nothing downstream needs it until more has accumulated, so it can sit open with no consequence.

The state machine, per event:

| Event | Open turns | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_prompt` | 0 | open a new turn, stamp the prompt with it |
| `user_prompt` | 1 | close the open turn, open a new turn, stamp the prompt with it |
| `user_prompt` | more than 1 | hard error: the thread is in an invalid state |
| `turn_end` | 1 | close the open turn |
| `turn_end` | 0 | disregard |

Closing a turn, by either trigger, fires its asynchronous derivation. The more-than-one-open case is a hard error during this phase rather than something swept under the rug, so an invalid thread is caught and triaged instead of producing quietly wrong turns later. A `turn_end` with nothing open is inert and is disregarded, since it changes no membership and corrupts no state.

### Token estimates

Part of the synchronous creation of messages is stamping each one with a token estimate of its original content. Doing this in the hot path means every message carries a size the moment it lands, with no later pass to count text and no API round trip. A turn carries the sum of its messages' estimates when it closes, so a turn's size is known the moment its membership is settled. These estimates are of the original message, not of any later compressed or lower-band form, which carry their own counts on the derived artifacts.

The method starts with a local tokenizer (tiktoken with the `o200k_base` encoding) and stores that count as the base. The base is stable and reproducible: the same text always yields the same number, with no provider call and no failure mode.

A local base count is an estimate, not an exact count for any given target model, since each model tokenizes a little differently. To get closer for a specific model, a per-model weight scales the base count, for example a code-heavy multiplier and a prose multiplier per provider and model. The weights come from offline calibration that runs representative content through the base tokenizer and through the target model's tokenizer and takes the ratio. The base count stays stored as the source of truth; model-specific estimates are the base scaled by a weight at read time. This keeps the stored number stable while letting estimates retarget to whatever model matters, and it lets a later auto-compact re-band a thread for a target model from the stored base counts without recounting. Building the weight tables is a later concern; the base count is what intake assigns now.

### What the result reports

The result reports, per event, whether it was recorded, skipped as a duplicate, or rejected. A rejected event stops the batch, and events already written in the same transaction are rolled back, so a batch either lands cleanly or not at all. The result also reports turn boundaries that the batch opened or closed.

Long Horizon Context (LHC) is a CLI and SDK for managing an agentic harness's context and history. It keeps the full message history of a conversation as a durable record, and from that record builds shorter, summarized views that a harness can load and work from.

## Basics

LHC is a stateless API: an SDK with a thin CLI over it. Each call takes what it needs, such as a thread id, a file path, or an input file, and operates on durable storage, so nothing is held open between calls. Agents can drive the CLI directly, and TypeScript apps can consume the SDK. A future app server can expose the same operations as endpoints.

## Key domains and entities

**Threads.** A thread is the durable container for one ongoing conversation between a user and an agentic harness, and each thread lives in its own file. The `threads` domain creates threads, keeps a registry of which threads exist and where their files are, and holds thread-level metadata and status.

**Intake stream.** As a harness runs, it produces a stream of events: user prompts, assistant text and thinking, tool calls and their results, runtime notes, and a marker at the end of each turn. The `intake-stream` domain takes these events in ordered batches, records them into the thread, updates the message view as it goes, and starts the downstream turn work.

**Messages.** A message is one unit of the conversation, such as a user prompt, an assistant response, or a tool result, built from blocks of text, thinking, tool calls, tool results, images, or files. The `messages` domain turns incoming events into this message-and-block view and lets you read, list, and search it. It is also where a person or agent can edit or prune the message history directly.

**Turns.** A turn is one full exchange: a user prompt and all the assistant and tool activity that follows it, up to the turn-end marker before the next prompt. The `turns` domain derives turns and groups them into chunks, and into larger containers above chunks, that feed summaries and recall. Turns are the base unit; chunks are containers of turns.

**Thread views.** A thread view is a summarized, harness-ready rendering of a thread, produced by a smart compact and arranged so an agent can resume the conversation without the full history. The `thread-view` domain generates these views, keeps them current as new events arrive, and lets them be inspected, customized, and written into a provider's file format. A harness either loads a view LHC has written or pulls the current view from LHC directly.

**Inspect.** The `inspect` domain looks at a thread as a whole, producing overviews, statistics, and reports across its messages, turns, and views. It reads and explains; it does not change the record. Where `messages` works inside the history, `inspect` reports on the state of it.

The `intake-stream` domain takes these events in and writes them into the thread in the order they happened. It is the only way thread content enters the system from a harness.

These flows are about how data moves, not about a user interface. The operations exist to record incoming events, keep the message view current, and drive turn boundaries so the thread stays in a coherent state. A thread is single-threaded by definition: one conversation, one stream, no concurrent writers. That lets the domain treat the incoming stream as an ordered time series and make boundary decisions from position in that stream.

### The stream contract

The harness owns sending a coherent stream. The domain does not reconstruct order or membership from a malformed stream; it records what it is given, in the order given, and fails loudly when the stream implies an impossible state.

The contract:

- send events in the order they happened
- send a `turn_end` when a turn is complete
- a thread has zero or one open turns at any time

### Taking in events

A harness sends a batch of one or more events for a thread. The thread id rides outside the batch, since every event in a batch belongs to the same thread. The SDK takes typed event objects directly; the CLI reads a JSON array of events on stdin, parses it at the edge, and calls the same SDK operation.

```
cat events.json | lhc intake-stream message-events --thread <thread-id>
```

The domain maps the thread id to its file through the threads domain, then writes the batch to the thread's database in a single transaction. For each event it assigns the next position in the thread's order, records it, and projects it into messages and blocks so the message view stays current. It returns a result describing what happened to each event.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as harness
  participant I as intake-stream
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  H->>I: message-events (thread id, events)
  I->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>I: file path
  I->>F: record events, project messages, update turns
  I-->>H: per-event result
```

Events carry an idempotency key from the harness. If an event with the same key was already recorded for the thread, it is skipped rather than written twice, so a harness that resends a batch after a failure does not produce duplicates.

### Turn boundaries are decided here, synchronously

Turn boundaries are decided in the hot path, as events land, while intake is the thing watching the ordered stream. This is what keeps turn membership correct: a message is stamped with its turn at the moment it is recorded, not inferred later against a stream that has moved on.

The deterministic work is synchronous: recording events, projecting messages, opening and closing turns, stamping each message with its turn, and assigning token estimates. The slow, non-deterministic work that a closed turn needs, such as smoothing, lower-band projection, and compression, is fired off to run asynchronously. Closing a turn settles its membership immediately; the derivation that trails behind operates on a turn whose contents are already frozen.

Two events move turn boundaries. A `user_prompt` opens a turn. A `turn_end` closes one. The asymmetry is deliberate: a prompt opens, an end only closes. After a `turn_end`, no turn is open and waiting, so the database does not hold a phantom empty turn between exchanges. Events that arrive after a `turn_end` and before the next prompt belong to no turn; they appear in the live message view but not in any turn.

Most turns in normal operation close because the next prompt arrived, not because of an explicit `turn_end`. The `turn_end` is the additional closer that lets the final turn close without waiting for a prompt that may never come. An open turn with no following prompt is simply not done yet, and nothing downstream needs it until more has accumulated, so it can sit open with no consequence.

The state machine, per event:

| Event | Open turns | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_prompt` | 0 | open a new turn, stamp the prompt with it |
| `user_prompt` | 1 | close the open turn, open a new turn, stamp the prompt with it |
| `user_prompt` | more than 1 | hard error: the thread is in an invalid state |
| `turn_end` | 1 | close the open turn |
| `turn_end` | 0 | disregard |

Closing a turn, by either trigger, fires its asynchronous derivation. The more-than-one-open case is a hard error during this phase rather than something swept under the rug, so an invalid thread is caught and triaged instead of producing quietly wrong turns later. A `turn_end` with nothing open is inert and is disregarded, since it changes no membership and corrupts no state.

### Token estimates

Part of the synchronous creation of messages is stamping each one with a token estimate of its original content. Doing this in the hot path means every message carries a size the moment it lands, with no later pass to count text and no API round trip. A turn carries the sum of its messages' estimates when it closes, so a turn's size is known the moment its membership is settled. These estimates are of the original message, not of any later compressed or lower-band form, which carry their own counts on the derived artifacts.

The method starts with a local tokenizer (tiktoken with the `o200k_base` encoding) and stores that count as the base. The base is stable and reproducible: the same text always yields the same number, with no provider call and no failure mode.

A local base count is an estimate, not an exact count for any given target model, since each model tokenizes a little differently. To get closer for a specific model, a per-model weight scales the base count, for example a code-heavy multiplier and a prose multiplier per provider and model. The weights come from offline calibration that runs representative content through the base tokenizer and through the target model's tokenizer and takes the ratio. The base count stays stored as the source of truth; model-specific estimates are the base scaled by a weight at read time. This keeps the stored number stable while letting estimates retarget to whatever model matters, and it lets a later auto-compact re-band a thread for a target model from the stored base counts without recounting. Building the weight tables is a later concern; the base count is what intake assigns now.

### What the result reports

The result reports, per event, whether it was recorded, skipped as a duplicate, or rejected. A rejected event stops the batch, and events already written in the same transaction are rolled back, so a batch either lands cleanly or not at all. The result also reports turn boundaries that the batch opened or closed.

## Messages

A message is the readable form of activity in a thread. The `messages` domain gives users, agents, and other domains a way to read the conversation record that `intake-stream` produced from incoming events.

Events and messages are different records. Events are the ordered source stream received from a harness. Messages are the normalized view created from those events so the rest of the system can read, search, edit, group, and assemble thread history. A `turn_end` changes turn state but does not need to appear as a visible message in the conversation.

### Messages and blocks

A message represents one meaningful piece of conversation activity, such as a user prompt, assistant text, assistant thinking, a tool call, a tool result, or a runtime note. Some messages are simple text. Others need more structure, so a message can contain one or more blocks.

Blocks keep the parts of a message separate when they need separate handling. Text, thinking, tool-call metadata, tool results, runtime notes, images, and files can each be represented as blocks instead of being flattened into one string. This lets the system preserve provider activity in a readable form while still keeping structured parts available to turns, thread views, and inspection.

### Reading messages

The messages domain lists, views, and searches messages for a thread. It is the lowest-level human-readable view of the conversation. A user or agent starts here when they need to inspect what happened before looking at turns, chunks, or thread views.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as CLI, UI, or agent
  participant M as messages
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  C->>M: list, view, search
  M->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>M: file path
  M->>F: read messages and blocks
  F-->>M: message view
  M-->>C: messages
```

Each message carries the token estimate assigned during intake. The estimate describes the original message content. Derived forms, such as smoothed turns or lower-band summaries, carry their own counts.

### Editing messages

Manual cleanup goes through messages, not `intake-stream`. Intake-stream records new activity from a harness; messages is where a person or agent can later correct, prune, or reorganize the readable conversation record.

A message edit can make derived objects out of date. Turns, chunks, and thread views that used the old message content need to be refreshed or marked stale. The messages domain records the edit and exposes enough change information for those downstream domains to keep their derived state coherent.

### How other domains use messages

Turns group messages into conversational turns. Thread-view uses messages directly, and through turns and chunks, when it assembles harness-ready context. Inspect reports on message counts, token sizes, edits, and derived-state freshness.

> Full tool results stay in the message record. Trimming happens only in a generated/materialized thread view.

That keeps the model clean:

- `messages` owns the original readable message/block record.
- `turns` owns turn/chunk derivation.
- `thread-view` owns what a harness actually sees.
- Tool-result truncation is a **view policy**, not a mutation of history.

The current extension sounds messy because the provider file is both “working context” and “stored transcript.” In LHC we should split that:

```text
canonical messages:
  full tool result retained

active thread-view:
  tool result may be truncated after policy threshold

provider materialization:
  written from the active thread-view
```

So the operation becomes something like:

```text
thread-view refresh/maintain active view
  -> read messages / turns / chunks
  -> assemble current view
  -> apply tool-result truncation policy
  -> materialize provider file if needed
```

The tricky part is that this has to happen in two modes:

1. **Active view maintenance**
   - after new message/tool activity
   - keeps the local CLI/provider file usable while the session is live
   - probably triggered by harness signals like message-end

2. **Smart compact / regenerated view**
   - rebuilds a new thread-view from canonical state
   - applies the same truncation policy during assembly

Those two paths must call the **same truncation function/policy**, or it will drift into hacks again.

A reasonable policy shape:

```text
tool result truncation policy:
  thresholdTokens: 32000
  toolResultCharLimit: 500
  marker: "..."
```

Algorithm, roughly:

1. Walk the ordered content of the thread-view.
2. Count tokens until the threshold.
3. After the threshold is reached, truncate `tool_result` blocks to 500 chars.
4. Preserve metadata saying the block was truncated from a fuller source block.
5. Never mutate the canonical message/block content.

Open detail we need to decide later:

- If a large tool result is the thing that crosses the 32k threshold, do we truncate that tool result or only later ones?
- Is the threshold based on original full content, or on already-truncated rendered content?
- Does the active view rewrite the whole file or only patch affected ranges?
- Is this triggered by every message-end, every intake batch, or a separate thread-view maintenance call?

My instinct:

- threshold should be computed against the **view source before truncation**, so the policy is deterministic
- truncation should be represented as view metadata, not just text replacement
- old already-truncated tool results should remain stable so prompt-cache churn is limited
- the provider file should be treated as materialized output, not authority

So for the docs, I would not touch Intake/Messages/Turns much for this. I’d capture it later in **Thread-view**:

> Thread-view may apply view-local retention policies, such as truncating older tool results after a token threshold. These policies reduce active context size without changing the canonical message history.

And maybe one sentence in Messages:

> Messages retain the original tool result content even when a thread-view later renders that result in truncated form.

We can inspect the extension later to learn the failure modes, but the LHC home for this is clear: **thread-view owns truncation because truncation is a harness-facing context rendering concern.**

{"isError":false,"outputText":"# Long Horizon Context: Domain Design

This document describes each domain in more depth: what it stores, the operations it provides, and the other domains it calls. It builds on the vocabulary in 01-core-concepts.md.

## Threads

A thread is the durable container for one ongoing conversation. The `threads` domain creates threads, tracks where they live, and gives the rest of the system a way to find a thread by id. Two SQLite databases sit behind it:

- A listing of all threads is stored in a **thread catalog** database, with one row per thread holding its id, file path, title, and cached info such as message and turn counts, status, and timestamps.
- Each thread's own database holds that thread's full record: its events, messages, turns, chunks, and views. Reading or changing a thread's contents means opening its file.

The thread file is authoritative for its own identity. It stores its thread id once, as identity metadata. The records inside it (events, messages, turns) do not each carry the thread id, because the file is the thread. The thread catalog is a convenience lookup over the thread files, not the authority; it can fall out of step with where files actually live and be refreshed from them.

### Creating a thread

`new-thread` creates a thread at a given file path, sets up the empty thread inside it, and adds a row to the thread catalog. It generates a thread id and records the id-to-path mapping. If a file already exists at the path, the operation fails instead of touching it.

```
lhc threads new-thread --file-path ./alpha.lhc
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as user or harness
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  participant R as thread catalog
  C->>T: new-thread (file path)
  T->>F: create empty thread
  T->>R: add row (id, file path)
  T-->>C: thread id
```

### Finding a thread by id

A thread id is the primary, stable key a caller holds. It survives the thread file moving, which a file path does not. Other domains work with thread ids, and when one needs to act on a thread, it asks the threads domain to resolve the id to its file, then opens it. This resolution is the threads domain's main service to the rest of the system.

How the threads domain resolves an id is its own concern and can change with the environment. In local CLI use it reads the thread catalog database; in a long-lived service it can hold the mapping in memory; in other deployments it can resolve through a different store. Callers above it pass a thread id and do not change. A caller that already holds a file path can pass the path directly and skip resolution.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as a domain with a thread id
  participant T as threads
  participant R as thread catalog
  participant F as thread file
  D->>T: map id to file path
  T->>R: look up id
  R-->>T: file path
  T-->>D: file path
  D->>F: open and act on the thread
```

### Browsing threads

A user who wants to see their threads starts at the threads domain. It lists threads from the thread catalog, searches across titles and metadata, and shows the high-level info for one thread without opening its file. From a list, a user picks a thread and drills into its messages, turns, or views through the other domains. The CLI presents this directly, and an SDK consumer can wire the same list, search, and show operations into a UI.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as CLI or UI
  participant T as threads
  participant R as thread catalog
  participant O as messages, turns, thread-view
  C->>T: list, search, show
  T->>R: read listings and cached info
  R-->>T: rows
  T-->>C: threads
  C->>O: drill into one thread
```

## Intake stream

As a harness runs it produces a stream of events. An event is one recorded thing that happened in the thread:

- `user_prompt`: a prompt from the user, or an automated prompt that stands in for one
- `assistant_text`: assistant output text
- `assistant_thinking`: assistant reasoning
- `tool_call`: a tool invocation
- `tool_result`: the result of a tool invocation
- `runtime_note`: a note from the harness or runtime
- `turn_end`: a marker that the current turn is complete

The `intake-stream` domain takes these events in and writes them into the thread in the order they happened. It is the only way thread content enters the system from a harness.

These flows are about how data moves, not about a user interface. The operations exist to record incoming events and coordinate the synchronous domain work that follows from those events. As it records the stream, `intake-stream` calls `messages` to create the readable message-and-block view and calls `turns` to open or close turn state. Those calls are in-process calls to the domain surfaces, not CLI calls or separate service hops.

A thread is single-threaded by definition: one conversation, one stream, no concurrent writers. That lets the domain treat the incoming stream as an ordered time series and make boundary decisions from position in that stream.

### The stream contract

The harness owns sending a coherent stream. The domain does not reconstruct order or membership from a malformed stream; it records what it is given, in the order given, and fails loudly when the stream implies an impossible state.

The contract:

- send events in the order they happened
- send a `turn_end` when a turn is complete
- a thread has zero or one open turns at any time

### Taking in events

A harness sends a batch of one or more events for a thread. The thread id rides outside the batch, since every event in a batch belongs to the same thread. The SDK takes typed event objects directly; the CLI reads a JSON array of events on stdin, parses it at the edge, and calls the same SDK operation.

```
cat events.json | lhc intake-stream message-events --thread <thread-id>
```

The domain maps the thread id to its file through the threads domain, then writes the batch to the thread's database in one coherent write flow. For each event it assigns the next position in the thread's order and records the source event. For events that produce readable conversation activity, it calls the `messages` surface to create messages and blocks. For events that affect turn state, it calls the `turns` surface to apply the open or close rule. It returns a result describing what happened to each event.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as harness
  participant I as intake-stream
  participant T as threads
  participant M as messages
  participant U as turns
  participant F as thread file
  H->>I: message-events (thread id, events)
  I->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>I: file path
  I->>F: record source events
  I->>M: create messages and blocks
  I->>U: open or close turn state
  I-->>H: per-event result
```

Events carry an idempotency key from the harness. If an event with the same key was already recorded for the thread, it is skipped rather than written twice, so a harness that resends a batch after a failure does not produce duplicates.

### Turn boundaries are decided here, synchronously

Turn boundaries are decided in the hot path, as events land, while intake is the thing watching the ordered stream. `intake-stream` calls the `turns` surface to apply the turn state machine and get the turn membership for message-producing events. This keeps membership correct: a message is attached to its turn when it is recorded, not inferred later against a stream that has moved on.

The deterministic work is synchronous: recording events, calling `messages` to create messages and blocks, calling `turns` to open and close turns, attaching messages to the current turn, and assigning token estimates. The slow, non-deterministic work that a closed turn needs, such as smoothing, lower-band projection, and compression, is fired off to run asynchronously. Closing a turn settles its membership immediately; the derivation that trails behind operates on a turn whose contents are already frozen.

Two events move turn boundaries. A `user_prompt` opens a turn. A `turn_end` closes one. The asymmetry is deliberate: a prompt opens, an end only closes. After a `turn_end`, no turn is open and waiting, so the database does not hold a phantom empty turn between exchanges. Events that arrive after a `turn_end` and before the next prompt belong to no turn; they appear in the live message view but not in any turn.

Most turns in normal operation close because the next prompt arrived, not because of an explicit `turn_end`. The `turn_end` is the additional closer that lets the final turn close without waiting for a prompt that may never come. An open turn with no following prompt is simply not done yet, and nothing downstream needs it until more has accumulated, so it can sit open with no consequence.

The state machine, per event:

| Event | Open turns | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_prompt` | 0 | open a new turn, stamp the prompt with it |
| `user_prompt` | 1 | close the open turn, open a new turn, stamp the prompt with it |
| `user_prompt` | more than 1 | hard error: the thread is in an invalid state |
| `turn_end` | 1 | close the open turn |
| `turn_end` | 0 | disregard |

Closing a turn, by either trigger, fires its asynchronous derivation. The more-than-one-open case is a hard error during this phase rather than something swept under the rug, so an invalid thread is caught and triaged instead of producing quietly wrong turns later. A `turn_end` with nothing open is inert and is disregarded, since it changes no membership and corrupts no state.

### What the result reports

The result reports, per event, whether it was recorded, skipped as a duplicate, or rejected. A rejected event stops the batch, and events already written in the same transaction are rolled back, so a batch either lands cleanly or not at all. The result also reports turn boundaries that the batch opened or closed.

## Messages

A message is the readable form of activity in a thread. The `messages` domain owns the message-and-block view of the conversation. It creates that view from source events, lets users and agents read it, and provides the place where later message-level edits happen.

Events and messages are different records. Events are the ordered source stream received from a harness. Messages are the normalized view created from those events so the rest of the system can read, search, edit, group, and assemble thread history. A `turn_end` changes turn state but does not need to appear as a visible message in the conversation.

### Creating messages

`intake-stream` calls the `messages` surface as it records incoming events. The message operation creates a message for events that should appear in the readable conversation and creates the blocks that belong to that message. It also stores the token estimate for the message's original content.

The same surface can be used directly by other callers when they need a message operation outside the harness intake path. The difference is the caller, not the domain ownership: `messages` still owns message creation, and `intake-stream` uses that operation in-process while coordinating an event batch.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant I as intake-stream
  participant M as messages
  participant F as thread file
  I->>M: create message from recorded event
  M->>F: write message and blocks
  M-->>I: message id and token estimate
```

### Messages and blocks

A message represents one meaningful piece of conversation activity, such as a user prompt, assistant text, assistant thinking, a tool call, a tool result, or a runtime note. Some messages are simple text. Others need more structure, so a message can contain one or more blocks.

Blocks keep the parts of a message separate when they need separate handling. Text, thinking, tool-call metadata, tool results, runtime notes, images, and files can each be represented as blocks instead of being flattened into one string. This lets the system preserve provider activity in a readable form while still keeping structured parts available to turns, thread views, and inspection.

### Tool results

A tool result is stored in two forms: the full original output and a shorter abbreviated form. Both are created when the message is created, so the abbreviated form is a deterministic, stored derivative rather than something recomputed on demand. The full form is the record and is never discarded. Thread-view chooses which form to show in a given view, keeping recent results full and abbreviating older ones.

### Token estimates

Each message is stamped with a token estimate of its original content when it is created, in the same synchronous step that writes the message. Stamping on creation means every message carries a size the moment it lands, with no later counting pass and no API round trip, and a turn's size is the sum of its messages' estimates as soon as the turn closes.

The estimate starts with a local tokenizer (tiktoken with the `o200k_base` encoding), and that count is stored as the base. The base is stable and reproducible: the same text always yields the same number, with no provider call and no failure mode.

A local base count is an estimate, not an exact count for any given target model, since each model tokenizes a little differently. To get closer for a specific model, a per-model weight scales the base count, for example separate multipliers for code and prose per provider and model. The weights come from offline calibration that runs representative content through the base tokenizer and through a target model's tokenizer and takes the ratio. The base count stays stored as the source of truth; a model-specific estimate is the base scaled by a weight at read time. This keeps the stored number stable while letting estimates retarget to whatever model matters, including letting a later smart compact re-band a thread for a target model from stored base counts without recounting. Building the weight tables is a later concern; the base count is assigned when the message is created.

### Reading messages

The messages domain lists, views, and searches messages for a thread. It is the lowest-level human-readable view of the conversation. A user or agent starts here when they need to inspect what happened before looking at turns, chunks, or thread views.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as CLI, UI, or agent
  participant M as messages
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  C->>M: list, view, search
  M->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>M: file path
  M->>F: read messages and blocks
  F-->>M: message view
  M-->>C: messages
```

Each message carries the token estimate assigned when the message was created. The estimate describes the original message content. Derived forms, such as smoothed turns or lower-band summaries, carry their own counts.

### Editing messages

Manual cleanup goes through messages, not `intake-stream`. Intake-stream records new activity from a harness; messages is where a person or agent can later correct, prune, or reorganize the readable conversation record.

A message edit can make derived objects out of date. Turns, chunks, and thread views that used the old message content need to be refreshed or marked stale. The messages domain records the edit and exposes enough change information for those downstream domains to keep their derived state coherent.

## Turns

A turn is one exchange in a thread. It starts with a `user_prompt`, or an automated prompt that stands in for one, and includes the assistant text, assistant thinking, tool calls, tool results, and runtime notes that follow. A turn closes when a `turn_end` arrives or when the next `user_prompt` starts a new turn.

The `turns` domain owns turn state, turn records, and turn-based containers such as chunks. It exposes the operations that open and close turns during intake, and it derives closed turns into the forms that later feed summaries, bands, and thread views.

### Opening and closing turns

`intake-stream` calls the `turns` surface as it processes incoming events. On a `user_prompt`, the turns operation opens a new turn, or closes the previous open turn and then opens a new one. On a `turn_end`, it closes the current open turn. If no turn is open, the `turn_end` is disregarded.

The open or close decision is synchronous. The result tells intake which turn, if any, a message-producing event belongs to. This is how messages get attached to a turn while the stream is still being recorded.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant I as intake-stream
  participant U as turns
  participant M as messages
  I->>U: apply boundary state for event
  U-->>I: current turn membership
  I->>M: create message with turn membership
```

### Deriving closed turns

Closing a turn makes its membership stable. The slow work that follows can run after the close: building the full turn record, smoothing the prompt or transcript, creating lower-band projection text, and preparing the turn for chunking. This work belongs to `turns`, even when it runs asynchronously.

A closed turn keeps enough source information to trace back to the messages and events it came from. That lets a later edit, repair, or inspection report explain which source messages contributed to a turn and whether derived state is current.

### Chunks

A chunk is a container of turns. Chunks let the system group multiple closed turns into larger units that can be summarized or placed into lower-fidelity bands. Turns are the base unit; chunks are the next container above them.

The `turns` domain owns chunk formation because chunking depends on turn order, turn size, and lower-band projection state. Thread-view later uses those chunks when it assembles a harness-ready context view.

### Reading turns and chunks

The turns domain lists and views turns and chunks for a thread. These operations are used by agents and users who want to inspect the conversation at a higher level than individual messages, and by thread-view when it needs turn and chunk material for context assembly.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as CLI, UI, or agent
  participant U as turns
  participant T as threads
  participant F as thread file
  C->>U: list or view turns and chunks
  U->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>U: file path
  U->>F: read turns and chunks
  F-->>U: turn and chunk data
  U-->>C: turns and chunks
```

## Thread view

A thread view is a summarized, harness-ready rendering of a thread. It holds enough of the conversation for an agent to resume work without the full history: recent activity at high fidelity, older activity compressed into shorter forms. The `thread-view` domain generates these views, keeps them current as new events arrive, and renders them for a harness to consume. A harness either loads a view that LHC has written to a file or pulls the current view from LHC directly.

A view is a rendering, not a second copy of the conversation. It is assembled from records the other domains already own: messages, turns, chunks, and the summaries derived from them. Producing a view never changes the canonical history; it selects and arranges what already exists.

### Bands

A thread view is arranged in bands of decreasing fidelity, from the most recent activity down to the oldest:

- **full**: recent turns rendered close to their original form
- **smooth**: smoothed turns, cleaned and attenuated but with their content preserved
- **detailed**: detailed summaries of older chunks
- **brief**: brief summaries of the oldest chunks, the compressed floor of the view

The bands are a gradient, not a cliff. As a turn ages it moves down a band, losing fidelity in steps instead of dropping out of the view all at once. The recent end stays sharp for the work in progress; the old end stays cheap while still carrying the shape of what came before.

### Generating a view

Generating a view, the operation a user sees as a **smart compact**, sets the band arrangement for the whole thread: which turns and chunks fall into which band, rendered into a current view. It works by selecting artifacts the other domains have already derived, not by recomputing them. The smoothed turns and chunk summaries exist before a smart compact runs, so generating a view is assembly, not summarization.

A smart compact runs periodically, not on every turn. Each one resets a large part of the view, so running it constantly would be costly for a harness that caches its prompt. Between compacts the lower bands hold still: the brief, detailed, and smooth arrangements settled at the last compact do not move. Only the full band changes between compacts, as new turns arrive at the recent end and the oldest full turns wait to be re-banded at the next compact.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as user, agent, or harness
  participant V as thread-view
  participant T as threads
  participant U as turns
  participant M as messages
  participant F as thread file
  C->>V: smart compact
  V->>T: map id to file path
  T-->>V: file path
  V->>U: read turns, chunks, summaries
  V->>M: read recent messages
  V->>F: write the current view
  V-->>C: view ready
```

### Assembling the active view

Between compacts, the view a harness consumes is assembled cheaply from the locked brief, detailed, and smooth bands plus the current full-fidelity tail of recent turns. Assembling it is deterministic local work, reads and rendering, with no provider calls and no summarizing. An extensible harness can pull the assembled view before each model call without paying to re-derive anything.

Assembly selects already-derived artifacts; it does not create missing ones. If a band depends on a summary that has not been derived yet, or that failed to derive, the view reports the gap rather than inventing the missing content or running repair in the hot path. Recovering missing derived state belongs to the domain that owns it, not to view assembly.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as harness
  participant V as thread-view
  participant F as thread file
  H->>V: pull current view
  V->>F: read locked bands and recent turns
  F-->>V: band artifacts and full tail
  V-->>H: assembled view
```

### Tool results in the active view

Tool results move through fidelity on a shorter cycle than the bands. A tool result is stored by `messages` in two forms, full and abbreviated, and `thread-view` decides which form a given view shows. Recent tool results show in full, because the agent is likely still working with them; older ones show abbreviated, because their full output is rarely needed once the work has moved on.

The decision is split into two steps to keep the view stable for a harness that caches its prompt. A tool result becomes **eligible** for abbreviation as it ages past a size threshold, but staying eligible does not change the view. Eligible results are **activated** to their abbreviated form in batches, every few turns or when the recent tail grows past its budget, rather than one at a time as each turn lands. Flipping results one by one would rewrite the prompt on most turns and invalidate the harness's cache each time; flipping a batch occasionally keeps the prompt prefix stable between activations. The thresholds and cadence are tunable; the architectural point is that abbreviation is a sticky, batched decision, not a fresh recomputation each turn.

### Rendering for a harness

The same assembled view renders in more than one form. An extensible harness that can take its context from LHC pulls the view as an in-memory message array. A closed harness that reads only its own session file gets the view written into that provider's file format. Both come from the same view; only the output form differs. A written provider file is a materialized rendering of the view, not a second source of truth: the thread file remains authoritative.

{"argumentsJson":{"content":"# Long Horizon Context (LHC) — Technical Architecture

## Status

This document defines the technical architecture for LHC. It establishes the system shape, core stack, and foundational decisions that all downstream epics and tech designs inherit. The domain model it builds on is defined in `../01-onboard/01-core-concepts.md` and `../01-onboard/02-domain-design.md`; those documents remain the authority on domain vocabulary and ownership.

---

## Architecture Thesis

LHC is a local-first TypeScript SDK with a thin CLI over it, built as one package organized by domain service surfaces. Each thread is one SQLite file; a registry database maps thread ids to files. Every operation is stateless: a call takes a thread id or path, opens what it needs, works, and returns. The hot path — event intake and view pulls — is synchronous, deterministic, and local; everything involving inference runs as durable deferred work owned by the domain that queued it. Domains call each other only through their public surfaces, enforced by import boundaries, so the same operations serve the SDK, the CLI, in-process cross-domain calls, and a future app server without divergence.

---

## Core Stack

| Component | Choice | Version | Rationale | Checked | Compatibility Notes |
|-----------|--------|---------|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Runtime | Node.js | >=24 | Built-in `node:sqlite` removes the native-dependency burden; modern ESM | 2026-06-09 | `DatabaseSync` exercised by the v1 reference build in this repo (31/31 green) |
| Language | TypeScript | ^5.9 | Strict typing is the SDK product surface | 2026-06-09 | `strict`, `NodeNext`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` |
| Package manager | pnpm | 10.x | Workspace root already established | 2026-06-09 | `packages/*` workspaces |
| Storage | `node:sqlite` (`DatabaseSync`) | Node built-in | One file per thread; zero install footprint for SDK consumers; synchronous API fits short-transaction design | 2026-06-09 | WAL mode + `busy_timeout`; stability status in Node 24 should be re-verified at first epic's tech design |
| Validation | Effect Schema (`effect`) | ^3.21 | Real decode/reject at the intake boundary with structured errors | 2026-06-09 | Scope pinned by prior decision: schema validation only; public APIs stay Promise/plain-object; no Effect SQL/queue/runtime |
| Token counting | `js-tiktoken` (`o200k_base`) | ^1.0 | Deterministic local base counts; pure JS, no native deps | 2026-06-09 | Base unit stored once; model-specific weights are derived later, never stored per-model |
| Tests | vitest | ^4 | Already in use; fast TS-native | 2026-06-09 | |
| CLI arg handling | `node:util` `parseArgs` + hand-rolled command routing | Node built-in | CLI is a thin adapter; a framework would invert that | 2026-06-09 | Revisit only if command surface outgrows it |
| Dev runner | tsx | ^4 | `dev:cli` ergonomics | 2026-06-09 | |

### Rejected Alternatives

| Considered | Why Rejected |
|-----------|-------------|
| better-sqlite3 | Native build/install burden on every SDK consumer; `node:sqlite` is sufficient and built in |
| One package per domain | Packaging ceremony before seams are stable; domains share transactions and an operation context. One package with enforced internal boundaries gives the protection without the friction |
| Effect-native public API (Effect SQL, PersistedQueue, Effect runtime in signatures) | Prior decision: Effect earns its keep at the validation boundary; a Promise/plain-object surface keeps the SDK consumable by any TS caller |
| Daemon / long-lived server process | Stateless per-call operations are the product stance; a server is a future adapter over the same SDK, not the core |
| JSONL / file-per-record storage | No transactions, no cheap indexed reads; SQLite gives both in one file per thread |
| Character-ratio token estimates | Proven unreliable in the POC; a real local tokenizer is cheap |

---

## System Shape

One package (`lhc`) exposing an SDK; the CLI is a thin wrapper over it; a future app server wraps the same operations. All state lives in SQLite files on local disk.

### Top-Tier Domains

| Domain | Runtime Surface | Owns | Depends On | Downstream Inherits |
|--------|----------------|------|------------|---------------------|
| `threads` | SDK + CLI | Thread creation, registry, id→file resolution, thread metadata | storage | Thread file is authoritative for identity; registry is a refreshable convenience index; id stored once in file metadata |
| `intake-stream` | SDK + CLI | Ordered event intake, stream contract, synchronous turn-boundary coordination | `threads`, `messages`, `turns` | All-or-nothing batches; idempotency keys; hot path is deterministic-only; intake coordinates but does not own message/turn mechanics |
| `messages` | SDK + CLI | Message/block records, token stamping, read/search, edits, message-level derivations (tool-result summaries) | `threads`, deferred-work, token-counting | Full record never destroyed; edits clear-and-regenerate; tool-result summary is a derivation with state, truncation is the deterministic fallback |
| `turns` | SDK + CLI | Turn lifecycle and state machine, turn derivations (smoothing, lower-band projection), chunks as an internal subdomain (formation, close, detailed/brief summaries) | `threads`, `messages`, deferred-work | Membership is stamped synchronously and frozen at close; chunk internals are not a public surface; band materials are served to thread-view on request |
| `thread-view` | SDK + CLI | View assembly, smart compact, band locking, tool-result visibility policy (eligible/activate), readiness sweep, rendering (message array + provider file) | `threads`, `messages`, `turns` | Views are derived and disposable; assembly is read-and-assemble only; missing derivations degrade, never block; thread-view drives repair through owning domains' surfaces and derives nothing itself |
| `inspect` | SDK + CLI | Read-only reports: composition, sizes, derivation health, view contents and cost | all domain surfaces | Never writes, repairs, or derives; reads only through domain surfaces |

**Technical capabilities** (not domains — no surface, no product vocabulary): **deferred-work** (durable per-thread ordered work queue) and **token-counting** (base-unit estimates). Domains use capabilities; capabilities never call domains or contain domain logic.
